utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. And good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll try our best to let you spend your weekend at home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would be grateful very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Alispahic. Now, yesterday I was asking you some questions about particular transcripts, and I wanted to ask you a couple of details about such transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown - just excuse me - Exhibit 436. Yes, Your Honours, I'm sorry. I don't believe this has been uploaded. We distributed copies of this yesterday. I don't know -- I think the witness probably doesn't have it in front of him here, so could the witness just be given the Bosnian copy, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I just ask that you -- I'm not going to ask you about the content of this document because you've made it clear that you as minister didn't normally have the job of looking at these documents. But I have another formal question to ask you and that is that on the front page of this document in the top right-hand corner there is certain writing. Would you mind just looking at the top right-hand corner there. And in particular it says the letters STR.POV. and then below that it says linija rada 02. Do you see those notations?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, the meaning of that marking 02 in professional terms was that the person who was subject to these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Morrissey, I'm sorry to interrupt you. It seems to me we did not get that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. And how about the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I think it was distributed both in English and B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The limited English version of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Alispahic. I'll just resume the question. That notation 02, does that mean that the person who was target of the -- of the operative measure of phone-tapping had the status of an internal enemy or potential internal enemy of the state?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I explain certain matters that I believe to be of key importance in this context in explaining this documentation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, it may be possible to have an explanation. I would just ask if, are you in a position to answer the question I asked, first of all, what is the meaning of that 02 number?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will reply to any question of yours to the best of my abilities. 02 stands for the line of work, the kind of work. And as for your suggestion that 02 stands for some kind of an enemy, be it internal or not, is something that I don't know and it is not immediately obvious based on this. Based on what is stated here in the heading, no conclusive opinion can be drawn on the status of the person against whom the measures of this service were implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You made it clear yesterday that you were a minister and not a technician. Is it known to you what the -- what this 02 number means in precise terms?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it stands for can be verified with this service. These figures and these marks are not permanent ones. They change from time to time. This is something that is regulated by regulations. Figures 02, 01, 03 are not fixed ones; that can be changed depending on the organisation of the service. What you need to do is check what at that period of time 02 stood for. Nowadays I'm sure that 02 stands for something else; you can verify this. I'm saying this because the same situation was when I took the job from my predecessor. At that time we also changed certain codes. So I assume that the same would apply nowadays as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, well I'm grateful for that explanation. And could I just ask you one step further. There must have been in existence at the time some sort of document which explained the meaning of these numerals, and can I ask you what would be the title of such a document and where would it be stored?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the general document, the rules on the internal organisation of the state security service. In this case it was the sector of the state security service. But I would still like to ask the Bench to allow me to give an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What is it that you want to give an explanation about? What topic is it that you want to give an explanation about?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely this topic, the documents that we are currently discussing. This is of procedural nature, of legislative nature. That's what I wanted to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps if you deal with the questions I have to ask you about these matters it may be that those questions cover what you want to say, and if they don't then could you indicate that there's something that we're missing that's important. And we'll see how far we can go that way. Very well. Well, thank you for that indication. Now, I just had some other -- I have one further question concerning that 02. You've indicated that -- in your evidence now that there would be -- that there's a general document, the rules on internal organisation of the state security service. But that document itself would not contain a precise explanation of the term 02 because the term 02, as you've indicated, is one that would change from time to time. And therefore --

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, you're not right. There are always explanations which define what 02 or other figures stand for. This is something which is always defined within the service. The code stands for a certain task. You just simply have to make a connection between the type of the task and the code.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. So that I understand you well, we can find the meaning of 02 in that particular set of rules to which you referred. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the enactment of the SDB you will be able to find what 02 stands for. The document will set forth this type of tasks is defined as 02.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And the final on that topic is that: To your recollection did the meaning of the term 02 change during your term of office as Minister for the Interior or did it maintain the same meaning from the start to the finish?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say. I don't remember whether there were any changes during that period of time. A lot of time has passed since then. That was directly under the responsibility of the chief of the SDB, therefore I really couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And which particular chief of the SDB are you referring to? Are we speaking there of Mr. Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Jozo Jozic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And later on Nedzad Ugljen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. You're right. Very well. I just have a couple of other questions to ask of a professional nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown -- I'm sorry, just excuse me, I just want to select the document to be provided. Your Honours, what is to be shown to the witness here is the rule on the work of the SDB adopted in August 1992 by the Ministry of Interior Affairs at the time. That was not this witness; it was before he was there. Now, this document is not uploaded, it is not translated -- pardon me, it is translated. It is not proposed to rely upon or take the witness through document after document about it. And as I say, it's a lengthy document. There are certain questions I want to put to him about it of very much a formal nature just to indicate what the rules were and to make them available, should anyone need to look at them. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Alispahic, what's about to be shown to you is a document I think authorised by your predecessor, Mr. Pusina, and I just ask you to look at it and confirm what it is.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Morrissey, this document will be MFI 438.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I won't ask you to read the whole thing, but if you wouldn't mind flicking to see if it appears to be a familiar document to you and then to indicate to the Court -- indicate to the Tribunal what that seems to be.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it would be proper for me to say whether I am familiar with the rules or not. I think that there should be some supporting documentation with these rules which would state that it was in force during a certain period of time. I think that within the SDB one could obtain documentation going to the validity of this document. I think that from a professional standpoint it would be improper for me to interpret the rules of -- on internal organisation of the SDB, which was a document in force even before I came to office. In addition to that, I would like to ask the Honourable Trial Chamber not to require me to draw some conclusions, which would be improper. These are highest-ranking documents within the SDB. The documentation that is being shown to me here for the first time is something that cannot be seen outside of the service. These are secret documents, and if such secret documents are being shown to me, then there should be some supporting documentation explaining how this came to be in your possession. Therefore, Your Honours, it is not up to me to assess whether there is a valid document, whether this is an authentic document; this is something that you should ask the service to confirm. The service that provided the documents should also be able to give a confirmation of the authenticity of these documents, because if you ask me to do that then I would have to engage in speculation and that would only produce negative effects. It could cause damage and I think that it would direct the proceedings in the wrong direction. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, I believe that the Defence counsel just want to know how much you know about this document. We'll see how far you could go. If you cannot answer certain questions or maybe some issues are out of your knowledge, just tell us. There's no problem about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. But, Mr. Alispahic, it's -- I understand why you raise those matters. From a security point of view, if you see a -- if you see something that's potentially damaging to the organisation or that should not be discussed in public, you should tell us that straight away because there is an ability to move into the private session here where such things will not then be broadcast to the public. However, I'll just persist with a formal question here at the moment. The document there, I do not ask you to interpret it or to look at it -- or to give any legal opinions. What I wish to ask you is: Do you recall whether that document was in operation at the relevant time, which for our purposes is 1993?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly couldn't say. I couldn't reply to your question whether precisely this -- these rules were in force in 1993. What I can say is that there always was in existence such a document, the rules of the service. But as to which particular document was in force at which particular time, I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And I take it what you would also say is that the Bosnian government would be in a position to provide some documentation as to when a particular set of rules was in force and when it ceased to be in force?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the state security service, one should be able to find all sets of rules which were in force in different periods of time; this is something that could be established easily. They could give you an answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm grateful for the -- for your persistence with this. And I have one further question and that is: When you mentioned the document that explains what is the meaning of 02, were you referring to this document or whichever document it was that succeeded this document in your time as minister or are you referring to a completely different set of rules?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that these were the rules on internal organisation of this service. What you have here are the rules on the work of the SDB which provide a framework for methods and -- that are applied in work, whereas internal organisation is quite another matter. The rules can define certain segments of work; however, internal organisation, I think, defines what 02, 03, et cetera, stands for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Just excuse me one moment, Mr. Alispahic. I just have to raise something with the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the circumstances of that, I won't seek to tender this document because the witness has made it clear he can't say that it was in force at the relevant time. We really have to make further inquiries about this issue, and the matters have been put to this witness because he's the only witness called who would appear to be capable of saying anything about it, but he's given his answer so I do not offer this document for tender at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for that. I just have to put a couple of other transcripts before you now in the same way that I put the transcript yesterday concerning Mr. Halilovic and General Jasarevic. If you haven't seen the document before, tell us; and if you don't remember the contents of the document, you also should tell us that. But we wish to put them into evidence here, and therefore I'm going to show them to you and you can comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, first of all, could the witness please be shown Defence document D408A. That is uploaded and it's DD00-1779.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI 439.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have a hard copy -- because this runs over four pages, we've got a hard copy of this for the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Alispahic, do you have on the screen in front of you now a copy of a transcript dated 24th of --

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Now, this is a conversation that occurs on the 24th of September, 1993, between Ismet Dahic and Sefer Halilovic. And I just wanted to ask you first of all before I come to the document, Ismet Dahic, as you recall, was the deputy of Vahid Karavelic within the military structure of the 1st Corps. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's right, but please don't ask me to confirm with certainty what role Dahic had at the time. I suppose you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. And again, I make it clear that given your answers yesterday we don't presume that you've seen this document before, but we have to ask you whether you have. So would you mind just having a look at it and if you remember seeing it before tell us; and if you haven't seen it before or you don't recall, tell us that too, please.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never seen this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, nevertheless, I'll just ask you whether you're familiar with any of the information in it from other sources; in other words, whether your memory tells you that you can recall this incident. Perhaps about six or seven lines from the bottom there's a comment here from Mr. Dahic where he says -- where he's asked, sorry -- or he says this: "These units were available" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is at the bottom of page 1 of the English transcript and it says -- I'm probably going now about 10 lines from the bottom or perhaps even a bit more, 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: "These units were available. The deltas have refused. They never even responded, won't speak to me -- the duty officer won't speak to me. He hung up on me last night. The commander isn't returning my calls." Sefer says: "Uh-huh." And Dahic says: "These here have agreed and so has Mujo, 125 men as agreed. We talked to them and they were about to set off last night but the 9th has refused. There are no available troops from other units." And Sefer's then recorded as saying: "Fuck it, what shall we do?" Now, just from your own subjective memory, does this ring a bell? Do you recall this incident where Halilovic and Dahic were trying to get troops to go and having trouble, as described here?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't give you any comments, either in relation to this document or to its contents. This is the first time I've seen this document, and the best I can tell you is that this is a reflection of what was going on in Sarajevo at the time, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, thank you for that comment. And because of that answer, I'll move on to the next one and ask you exactly the same questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown D408B. This also is uploaded. It's DD00-1785.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Alispahic, while that's being brought up, I'll just explain, this is a similar document between the same two people, and I just ask you to look at it. And do you have that in front of you now, that document?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI 440.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Is the situation the same with this document, you haven't seen it before?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Would you just mind repeating your answer, please; the interpreter didn't get it.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. Very well. I won't ask you any further questions about that document, frankly. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness now please be shown another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I have about six of these to put to you one after the other in the same way that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: So the next one is D323. This document is not uploaded, so we'll have to provide hard copies to everyone, which we'll do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: While this is arranged I'll explain what is coming. This is another similar transcript, this time dated the 9th of October, 1993. This one is a conversation -- it's a short conversation between Stjepan Siber, who was a deputy commander of the army at the time, and Sefer Halilovic. And I'll ask you exactly the same questions: Have you seen it before? Do you remember the incident? And you simply tell us what you remember about that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI 441.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Would you mind just taking the chance briefly to look at that and seeing if you recall seeing this transcript before.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is the first time I see this document. Should I go through it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: If you wouldn't mind just briefly looking to see whether it helps your memory. You may remember such an incident, as is described in there, or you may not. And if you remember it, tell us; and if you don't, tell us that, too.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I have never seen the document before. What it talks about doesn't ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And there was no need for -- very well, I withdraw that. Very well. Thank you. Could I just ask you as a question of form and the form of the documents you've been shown, the two Dahic documents and this Siber document, do they appear to you to be the products of the same process of phone-tapping that we've discussed yesterday and today?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say either way, but it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: At all events do you agree that the documents appear consistent with that conclusion? And I mean in a formal sense, not in terms of their content.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These documents -- this document looks very much like the ones we've looked at. It belongs to the same group of documents, but I must express a reservation with regard to all these documents as long as there's no explanation that would go to their authenticity, like I said at the outset. This is just an assumption on my part, but it's something you may be interested in. I think it talks about measures applied against General Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Well, we understand you personally did not review these documents, and therefore we don't ask you to authenticate them yourself. Is that a fair way to put the matter?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely what I said, and I'll repeat it. There's a procedure precisely for this kind of document for perfectly understandable reasons, human reasons, and technical reasons. This is the sort of measure that can be applied against anyone, but there are certain procedures to follow. And the same applies to these documents being produced. All you could find in the file is a list of persons, but never anything else in relation to the state security or the intelligence service. Everything else would imply that there was a procedure in place and how this -- these documents were to be used. I'm telling you about this as a matter of principle, that there had to be a procedure according to which these documents were compiled and used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, thank you for that explanation. Very well. Thank you. Now, that completes for the moment the questioning concerning the telephone transcripts, and I wish to turn now to another measure. Mr. Alispahic, yesterday you were shown a document which was the decision signed by you concerning measures against -- or concerning measures about General Halilovic. And at that time, two measures were authorised, the zolja measure and another measure called the agava measure. Now, was the agava measure a different measure involving the placement of listening devices within physical locations such as offices or other such places?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't talk about the definition of the agava measure, whereas the previous measure was used more frequently and that's why I remember it more clearly. But all measures change over time and their names change in order to protect the secrecy of these measures, and this is the reason why I can't comment on specific documents or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I understand that and I wasn't proposing to ask you to comment on specific documents. Just on the terminology question, in the case of Mr. Halilovic the phone-tapping method was called zolja, but --

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: But I take it from what you say that the terminology your service used to describe phone-tapping changed over time, too. Is that correct? Sometimes it would be zolja; sometimes it would be another name?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The name of that measure changed frequently over time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, as to agava, as a matter of principle I think you've made it clear you don't recall exactly what that involved. Could I just ask you -- I'll ask you to look at a document now that we're going to show you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: We don't have this uploaded, but this is Defence document D816, and we'll just circulate copies of this. I think it would be MFI 442.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What's going to be shown to you now - it's being circulated around the room - but there's -- this is a photocopy of what seems to be a map of Mr. Halilovic's office. I'LL just ask you to take a moment to look at that and familiarise yourself with it while I explain something to the Judges at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is a rough translation -- when I say "rough," we hope it's not rough but we hope it correct. It's done by a team member here not by CLSS. It was done I believe yesterday or the day before. It's simply is a translation of the terms used on the previous page. You'll see on the left there's a list 1 to 9 -- sorry, 1 to 10. And this is -- sorry, 1 to 10, pardon me. It goes down to 9 at the bottom and then 10 is to the right of that. And that list is translated on the following page. And I'm reminded that there's an official translation of this pending and we'll provide that as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Thanks. Now, what -- first of all, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Have you seen documents of this form before, not necessarily connected with Mr. Halilovic but concerning the placing of listening devices in other cases?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was a long time ago while I was still working as an operative for the state security service. I saw documents like this one. These documents were produced by people from a technical department within the state security. This was not done by operatives; these were purely technical matters. So I think there were very few people who were ever in a position to look at these documents. It's been 15 or 20 years since I last saw one like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. This document does not have a date on the face of it. Are you able to say by reference to this document the time period in which -- well, perhaps I'll ask you another question first. Is this document consistent with the measure agava which was proposed against -- proposed concerning Sefer Halilovic in the order signed by you? In other words, was Mr. Halilovic's room subject to listening device measures?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you the sort of specific answer that you expect, but I can give you my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And we can see how far that will take us or how useful you find it. This is a document that indicates that there's a plan for a room to be bugged or that it has already been done. What that says to me is that this measure that you refer to as agava is a measure to bug a room. That's what I can conclude based on this document and based on our previous discussion. I couldn't commit myself on anything else. I couldn't say whether it was done before, at this time, or after, or whether it was ever actually applied at all. I simply can't say. If the measure was applied, then probably this was done. If not in that case, well, I don't think I could possibly comment. But if I may, this is also within the sphere of operative work. This is a very complex measure. It's not particularly simple to apply, and sometimes teams simply give up because things happen that they can't control, and the result is it becomes impossible to take the measure. But if we're asking ourselves whether this measure was applied or not, it must be possible to establish that in some way, this certainly not being one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I understand that. Thank you for the clarifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I offer that document for tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, would you please provide us with some information concerning of the source and chain of custody of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I've got a general answer. I'll just see if I can get a more specific one. If you'll just excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document was provided by the organisation FOSS to the Defence some five months ago. That's the chain of custody that we have about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, not really. Just a question as to the relevance of it to the proceedings. I'm still unsure whether it's referring to a listening device or telephone interception. There's been a fair bit of evidence about telephone interception. I think the witness mentioned in part -- I think he said it was a listening device, but I'm not sure from looking at the document whether it was actually a listening device or telephone interception. But in any event, we probably don't object, we just question the relevance to the proceedings of this particular document. Perhaps that could be explored, though, whether it's a listening device or an intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, the Bench believes that this document will help us to understand and to consider the admission of all those intercepts. So we believe in this sense it's a relevant document. Since there's no serious objections from the Prosecution, this document is admitted into the evidence with the official translations; I believe that will be checked by this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honours, as soon as we have it, we'll forward it. And to the extent that it conflicts with our translation here, the official one should prevail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, some final questions on that topic. And, Mr. Alispahic, you yourself are not aware of any material produced by the agava method in relation to Mr. Halilovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: In the circumstances of surveillance of Mr. Halilovic, it was a perfectly logical thing for the service to do, to place a listening device -- or attempt to place a listening device in his office. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't comment on that. Those who decided on the application of the measure -- I merely studied the measure. But those who decided on its application made the call as to which measures would be applied against General Halilovic eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. Is it within your knowledge whether a listening device was placed in any car or vehicle used by Mr. Halilovic in August and September 1993?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Is it within your knowledge whether a listening device was placed in any other location -- well, I withdraw that question. I'll ask a more specific one. Is it within your knowledge whether a listening device was placed at the IKM, the -- the location which you indicated you visited, in Jablanica in September of 1993?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that there was a location, as you say, at the IKM, forward command post. What I can say is link these statements to the general or Skup, as the code-name implies or to a more general context. If you want my opinion based on information that I had as a member of the Ministry of the Interior, I don't think they had adequate equipment at the forward command post to begin with, not that I'm an expert but I'm just trying to help. As for the location itself, I'm not familiar with any measures being taken there. I never received any reports to this effect, and it would have constituted a technical matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: In whose -- who did have responsibility for deciding whether or not to place such a listening device at the IKM at the operative level? Who had to make that decision?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military and intelligence bodies. I'm not sure about the level, whether corps level or the level of the unit in question. I can't possibly be more specific when it comes to the army. I can't say how exactly measures were applied there or at what level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Alispahic, you've been patient in answering these questions, and I've nearly finished this part of the cross-examination now. The last thing I want to ask you about concerns how the material gained by application of the zolja method was passed over to the military security service? In other words, how did your service pass that over? So my first question is: Who was responsible at the SDB for passing that material over to the military? Was that Mr. Ugljen?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: U-g-l-j-e-n, that's the spelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's what I thought it was. But in any event, is that the person?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the number one man of the service. He had the closest cooperation with other services, specifically the military intelligence service. If assistance was provided to the army applying these measures, then certainly each and every document you've shown me should be recorded somewhere in the archives and it should say exactly who received the relevant document. Someone from the service who was in charge of General Halilovic, for example, and then this person would pick up the transcripts and conversations. These, after all, were the people who used these measures for their own end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. At that time can you recall -- well, we've had some evidence from General Jasarevic here in this Tribunal already, and he explained to us the structure of his office. And he indicated that he had about 30 people working for him. Could I ask you: Does that accord with your recollection of the situation, that his staff in Sarajevo at the SVB, and in particular the UB, consisted of about 30 staff members?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I really can't say more about that. I've no idea how strong the security service or the security administration were. I'm not familiar with the way these services were organised, nor did I have any free time on my hands to deal with these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No. I understand that and you've made yourself clear about that, too. So in terms of the person to who Mr. Ugljen gave the documentation, do you know the identity of that person?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know the name of the person who directly and frequently communicated and/or received such information or documents. We had cooperation on several levels. There was cooperation between the services, between the SDB chief, Ugljen, and Jasarevic, and before Jasarevic, there were offices from the state security service. And there was cooperation on the lower level of the SDB and the military bodies in the field and in Sarajevo, alike. If there was communication in Sarajevo, it could have been with Mujezinovic, who was the centre chief at the time. There could have been communication regarding operative activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And one final question coming from that. Contacts at the high level between Mr. Ugljen and Mr. Jasarevic can be distinguished from contacts at a lower, more local and operative level between employees of each service. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. What they define would eventually lead to what you are discussing right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Well, thank you for those answers. Now I need to move to a new topic -- oh, sorry, there is one -- there is one residual one. I've forgotten about that. Apart from the measures zolja and agava that are mentioned in that document, was it also -- was it also within the discretion of the person organising these measures, in this case possibly Mr. Ugljen, to adopt other measures as well, such as personal physical surveillance, following of General Halilovic, and so on?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All measures which are regulated by various regulations and can be applied within the security service, including the military security service, can be used at the discretion of the chiefs of these services. I'm going -- I'm speaking now in general terms --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- not specifically regarding General Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, now I understand you're speaking at that level of generality. You've indicated that the military security service needed your organisation to help because you were technically better equipped than the SVB. When it comes to physical surveillance, having operatives follow a particular target and so on, did the SVB from the military need your help with that sort of thing, or were they able to do that much on their own?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember whether the SVB asked for assistance from SDB in any other field except for the technical measures. I don't remember them asking any other kind of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. And another, if you like, formal matter. In the case where operatives of the SDB are used in such surveillance activities -- in fact, I'll withdraw that question. I'll ask you a more general one. Where SDB operatives are involved in measures of any sort against a particular target, is it necessary for the SDB to retain a list of those operatives on the file? For example, in the case of General Halilovic, was it necessary for the SDB to maintain a list of those operatives who were concerned in the measures against him?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within its structure, the service has a department where there are a number of officers of the secret service who do exclusively that type of work. That measure is a lower-ranking measure in terms of other technical measures that require approval. And the employees who do that kind of work are identified by their first name, last name, and affiliation to that department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And just finally, it's necessary for a copy of a document with those names on it to be preserved in the archives at the technical section. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either the activities of that department or the names have to be recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And they have to be recorded in a document that is stored at the archives. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the reports coming from that surveillance apparatus normally are sent to an operative who follows the target. And this is stored in the archives, either in that file or in another file. These people finish their task, write up a report, and that's it. It is possible that they have a logbook where this information is recorded in rough terms. I have never engaged personally in that type of work, therefore I'm not very familiar with the technical methodology.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No. I'm grateful to the assistance you've given, and that is the end of those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Alispahic, I wish to turn to some narrative matters on how this case unfolded and your memory in the best way that you can give it. Were you ever shown by the Prosecutors -- or perhaps first of all. Were you ever shown at the time, that is in August and September 1993 -- I think I'll show you the document first and then I'll ask you if you've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just excuse me one moment. Could the witness please be shown Exhibit 146.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What I'm going to show you now is an order appointing Sefer Halilovic in charge of an inspection team consisting of himself, Mr. Karic, Mr. Suljevic, Mr. Bilajac, a security officer named Namik Dzankovic and two other individuals who play no part in these proceedings. I'll just ask you whether you've ever seen that before. Do you have that order on the screen?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have it yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Neither do we. Do you have it now? Now, Mr. Alispahic, I'm not going to ask you for a military expert opinion here, but I just wanted to ask you: Have you ever seen that document before?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Did the Prosecutors not show you this document at any time during the investigation?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've never seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And let me ask you: Was there any necessity for you as Minister of the Interior to be shown such a document back in August/September of 1993?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, very well. Well, I won't ask you to consider the text of it. The only thing I'd ask you to note is the date there. Do you see that it's dated at Sarajevo, 30th of August, 1993? And I'm looking at the top left-hand part. Do you observe that date?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Was -- were you aware of the -- the process by which Mr. Halilovic -- well, I withdraw that. Did you know that he was appointed the head of an inspection team at the time or was that level of detail not necessary to be provided to you at the time?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see why would the army send this type of an order to me? They didn't normally send such documents to me. So it's not up to me -- up to me to say. It was up to them to decide whether they would send something like this to me or not. I never really focussed on the role of General Halilovic and his function. It was not necessary for me to know that some kind of an inspection team was established, led by General Halilovic. I don't think I needed to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, I -- well, that's the -- that also is the proposition I was going to put to you. In light of that -- nevertheless, you gave evidence earlier in the week that you considered or it was your view that Sefer Halilovic was the commander of this operation, and I have some questions for you on that topic. First of all, you indicated -- and I just want to confirm that this is the reasons why you gave that evidence. You indicated that you gave that evidence because of things that were said at the Zenica conference. Is that correct? I'm going to put a number of these things, but first of all Zenica was one basis for that opinion that you had. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that General Halilovic was the commander of that operation based on several things, including the meeting in Zenica where the general explained why the operation was needed. Then I was also asked to allocate a special unit to be resubordinated in that operation. In addition to that, I knew that General Halilovic was the chief of the Main Staff. I also was familiar with the communications with the IKM or forward command post. Then I went, myself, to the forward command post. It was no weekend cottage; it was a typical forward command post. Being under oath now and wishing to state only the truth, I couldn't tell you now that I ever saw a decision appointing General Halilovic commander of that operation. However, the fact that the operation was indeed implemented and that I knew all other things point in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I understand that. And I'm just going to ask you about some of the specific bases one after the other that you've given and put some questions to you about them. And the first ones concern the meeting at Zenica. You've indicated that Sefer Halilovic raised the issue at Zenica. Could I ask you: What was the reaction of the other generals who were present at Zenica to Sefer Halilovic's proposal? In other words, was it a popular move? Was it unpopular? What do you recall about that?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when all of these discussions were held, these issues were debated, and the meetings which I attended allowed me to infer or understand how important it was to launch such combat activities and to liberate the territory. I think that even if we disregard other facts, it is undoubtable that General Halilovic was a much more prominent figure than any other commanders. He was a much more charismatic figure. And personally, I and other leaders always treated his proposal, suggestions, with respect. In addition to what I have stated previously, based on that and everything else I understood that General Halilovic was the commander of the operation and the number one man in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: So I understand what you say about that, but I have to ask you perhaps some more precise questions about the Zenica meeting. Do you recall the presence at that Zenica meeting of a man called Salko Gusic, who was the commander -- and in fact the relatively new commander of a new corps, the 6th Corps?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly -- I truly couldn't claim with any certainty that it was Salko Gusic. As I saw things, he was a lower-ranking officer in the army, lower than others who attended the meeting. I hope he will not take this as an insult, Salko Gusic, but other officers I knew much more and they ranked much higher at the time, were much more established, whereas Salko Gusic was just appearing on the scene, so to speak. That's really all I can tell you because I have no additional information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, that's okay. Are you able to recall how Salko Gusic responded to Sefer Halilovic's proposal, that there be an operation in Herzegovina, at the Zenica meeting?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall. I would like to remind the Defence that the meeting was recorded, both on audiotapes and videotapes. So perhaps you could use that material to find answers you're looking for. Your Honours, I was an observer there, somebody who came to see and hear what was going on and what needed to be done further. I was not in the same position as active army members. I did not have an active role. I had a small minor task to participate and assist to the extent of my abilities and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And I make it clear, there's no criticism of the role that you played at this meeting at all, Mr. Alispahic, but I have to ask you some details because we have witnesses -- evidence from other witnesses in the case. You recall that Arif Pasalic, the commander of the 4th Corps, was present. Do you remember how he responded to Sefer Halilovic's proposal at the Zenica meeting?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Arif Pasalic, as commander of the corps -- and please, you have to analyse my position from another angle as well. All officers attending meetings normally have their logbooks, their diaries where they record things that transpire. Therefore, it is much easier for them to explain and to recall what happened at a particular time, whereas I, as an interior minister, did not have any such diary or a logbook where I would record my activities. Our work procedures are different. And when I left the ministry, I didn't take with me any documents, any diaries or logbooks that army officers have and which could help me reconstruct the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Of course we understand that. If we could just come back to the Arif Pasalic issue. How did he respond at Zenica to the suggestion or proposal that you've described of General Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't remember Pasalic's reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: But Pasalic was present, I take -- or Pasalic and all of these generals were present at the time when Sefer Halilovic made this proposal. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody was present the entire time, at least that's as far as I can remember. Perhaps somebody did leave the conference room for an hour to attend to something else, but that's all I could tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And do you remember whether General Halilovic tabled any paperwork or plans concerning this proposal at the Zenica meeting in that conference room?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that General Halilovic presented any such paperwork. However, I do remember that there were various discussions which also focussed on various problems. Not everybody had the same viewpoint and position as to how things ought to be done. Officers had different views, and they elaborated on their views in military terms. I did not understand that completely. Therefore, I didn't really go into the depth of what they were saying; it was beyond me. If a commander was speaking about a battalion or brigade or an artillery unit, this is not something that I fully understand. Therefore, I didn't really focus, I didn't pay so much attention to what the army people were saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I understand your account. Thank you. Could you indicate with respect to the resubordination of the Laste Unit whether you provided to the Prosecutor any document concerning that.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until today, I never provided any documents to anyone. All documents relating to my position, my office, could be found at the Ministry of the Interior. I know for a fact that a dispatch or an order, whichever way you want to define it, was sent from the Ministry of the Interior about the deployment of that unit where various elements of that deployment were specified, the date of deployment, accommodation, and so on. So I would urge you to look for that document in order to fully grasp the role of the police within that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And we don't have that document here, Mr. Alispahic, so I have ask you the questions to answer as best you can now after these many years. And the question is: Do you recall the date or the approximate date of that written document?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the document had to be signed by Munir Alibabic, chief of the security services centre because Laste belonged to that centre. I, as a minister, was able to approve the participation of the unit in the operation, and that document had to be drafted in early September before they were deployed. I know that the document exists because the commander and his deputy told me about receiving a dispatch where this is defined. However, to this day I have not read that document, but it must exist because without that document the unit could not have been deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It ended up being the case -- perhaps I should ask you this -- no, I'll come to the question -- I'll come to the Mostar question in a few moments' time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm about to move to another topic now. Now might be a moment to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take a break and we'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm so glad that Mr. Weiner is present in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Thank you very much for welcoming me back. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And I might, I might, ask the parties to have a meeting this afternoon, but this hasn't been decided yet. But I just remind the parties to be available this afternoon. Yes, Witness, let's continue with the proceedings. Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you again, Mr. Alispahic. Very well. Now, I have to put some matters concerning the Zenica meeting to you and ask for your comments on these. Excuse me a moment, please. In these proceedings -- what I'm going to do is put an account of another witness here to you. In these proceedings we heard evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is at page 64 of the 4th of February of 2005, and it's from the evidence -- it's from the evidence of Mr. Gusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm going to read this evidence to you and then I'm going to ask for your comment about it. "Q. You can confirm, I take it, the following facts: No Operation Neretva 93 was mentioned at all. Is that correct? "A. The name of the operation was never mentioned. I did not hear it mentioned at the meeting. I did not hear the term "Neretva 93" mentioned at the meeting. "Q. The next point. Sefer Halilovic offered no plan at that meeting for an operation related to Mostar or indeed related to Herzegovina at all at that meeting. Is that correct? "A. As far as I remember, no, he didn't, not an operation. No. "Q. In fact, in a statement you made to the Prosecutors recently -- the most recent statement that you made you made the comment 'listening to the statements of General Sefer Halilovic during the meeting and on the recording I can see that his main focus was the warehouse in Zemunica, Hadzici, and an explosives factory in Vitez, Vitez being the priority. General Halilovic did not even mention Mostar. The situation in Mostar was presented by General Arif Pasalic.' And that's what you said to the investigators and that was the truth. Correct? "A. Yes, yes, yes. "Q. Okay. And at that meeting no one was appointed to command an operation in Herzegovina. Is that correct. "A. As far as I recall, that is correct. No one was appointed." Now, Mr. Alispahic, we have a problem because that's different to what you say. Can I ask you what you have to say about that difference?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The obvious difference is between my status and the status of the remaining officers who were present in Zenica. Secondly, the difference is I was only there for one day, and I was asked to resubordinate this special unit to them. Another thing I said in my testimony, and Gusic agrees, that I didn't hear the name of the operation used and defined in Zenica. It was never said that the operation would have this or that name or anything like that. What I testified reflects what I remember about this. I can't say more than that. I can't speculate about Gusic's statement. It is possible that Gusic's testimony related to their entire stay in Zenica. I also said that at the meeting I didn't hear that anyone was appointed as commander of the operation, and the same applies to General Halilovic. I also said my understanding of the meeting in Zenica was that a framework was defined for the operation that was to follow, and our own police unit was supposed to be part of this, about 50 strong. I said it then and I'm saying it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I understand that. But you also understand we have to put these materials to you. It's not fair to just leave them behind your back without giving you the chance to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And the next thing I'd ask is that the witness be shown Exhibit D109.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The Prosecutors have already shown you this document, Mr. Alispahic, but this is a document we've been calling the "Zenica Conclusions" dated 29 August and produced, as we understand, by Commander Delic. Do you remember being shown this document by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that was the first time I saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand that. But it's apparent on the face of the document that there's no reference to any operation to relieve Mostar nor to the appointment of General Halilovic to lead such an operation. Now, do you know why that is, if there was an operation -- an operational plan and -- sorry, I withdraw that. Do you know why that is at all?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question, but I can look at the context and try to answer your question. It's stated that I, the Minister of the Interior, was only there on the first day. It doesn't strike me as particularly important; there's only one line here mentioning that. I left after that, but I remember that I was supposed to be part of the combat operations to free the area, and General Delic and General Halilovic and all those present can confirm this. But my testimony now is that police involvement was requested to liberate the area around Mostar. I never said it was about Mostar itself; I was being quite specific. But combat operations were to take place that would liberate the area surrounding Mostar. Bearing in mind the difficult situation in Mostar itself from a military point of view, or at least that's how I understood what the soldiers were saying, that was the topmost priority at the time, to help that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I understand what you say about that, but I think we have to deal specifically with what Salko Gusic said. He specified in evidence what General Halilovic talked about at the Zenica meeting, and he specified a focus on Vitez -- I'll mention them again just so that we're clear, Vitez, and Zemunica, and Hadzici. He mentioned those three as being the areas that General Halilovic spoke about. But what you've said is that he spoke about an operation to liberate the area around Mostar. Now, that's a conflict we have to focus upon. Let me ask you this: Do you think at this distance in time many years ago, do you think your memory might be mistaken about what happened at Zenica, and in particular what Sefer Halilovic said about Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really think that at this meeting in part what was discussed was the problems in the Mostar and Neretva areas and the need to carry out combat operations in that area in order to liberate the area and in order to reopen communications with Mostar. I think that is what -- what was discussed. This may not have been a crucial issue at the meeting they had then, which was some sort of a conference really. Maybe these issues were relegated to the operative sectors within the army, but the reason I remember this is I was asked to participate, just that, nothing else. And I wasn't up to date about any of the plans that were or were not being prepared. I had no idea what the army was planning. It would have been impossible for me to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And we fully appreciate that's the case, and I'm not going to press you with questions about that. But I do have to press you with some other questions, and one concerns the videotape that was taken. Did the Prosecutors give you the opportunity to view that videotape before you gave your evidence here?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen any videotapes here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, rather than keeping us all here for five hours or so watching it, I'm going to put to you what's in it and if I put it wrongly the Prosecutor will correct that. But we've all -- we have that videotape; it's in evidence here. And Mr. Gusic had the chance to look at it before he gave his evidence and commented on it. Mr. Alispahic, that videotape reveals you, yourself, clearly indicating a concern for the plight [Realtime transcript in error "plot"] of Mostar and a need for the Bosnian armed forces to focus upon that area. And frankly, so far that's consistent with what you say here, that you were concerned by that. Do you remember expressing such a concern in the -- in the course of the meeting, saying that you thought there was a danger we'd fail the test at Mostar and that we should really focus on that area? Sorry, now we have a translation problem here. Before you answer that question, just excuse me a moment, it's been identified and I'm going to have to rectify it, so hold on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's a problem here, and I better record what it is. At page 39, line 1, the interpreter has recorded my question as referring to the "plot of Mostar," whereas in fact I referred to "plight." Plight, bad situation, in other words. The danger for Mostar. That would change the question -- the meaning of the question completely for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: So, Mr. Alispahic, forgive me, and I'm going to ask that question again and I'm going to use another word so the interpreter is not placed in a bad position by the Australian accent. Mr. Alispahic, the videotape which we're seeing here clearly reveals you expressing a concern for the dangerous situation of Mostar and a concern for the need to help in that area. We agree that's consistent with what you say up to now. But do you remember making comments to that effect in the meeting?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on information provided by the Mostar security services centre, I was aware of the fact that the situation was extremely difficult in the town of Mostar itself. They were facing great difficulty treating the wounded and putting up the wounded. They were facing a crisis regarding food supplies because the enemy forces were in control of the road into Mostar. As for all the ideas that people talked about, all the possible activities that were brought up, what I said was about that area, the Mostar area and to remain within that context, something to the effect that operations should be carried out to liberate the area. I said that the situation was disastrous and I can't reproduce this word for word, you must understand this. I proposed that the special unit be the first to be dispatched to Mostar to give them a hand with combat operations and to relieve the people down there who were extremely exhausted because they'd been involved in the operations for weeks and months by this time, while the other units were to carry out operations along the axis leading to Mostar. The other reason was really quite simple. The army, within the context of their own plans and operations and what they were supposed to do on the ground, that would only have entailed military units but no police units, and that was perhaps one of the reasons to have the special unit dispatched to Mostar. This was not discussed at any great length, but when I think back I think I said this to mean that those combat operations were necessary. I believed so at the time, and I still believed it was necessary at that point in time to carry out combat operations in order to relieve the situation of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I have two questions arising out of that. First of all, did you mention -- do you say you mentioned the Laste Unit by name at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. It's possible that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Second question: Do you recall whether the resubordination of that unit was discussed at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. It's possible that this was said in passing, but this was not a subject that was singled out for special treatment. That was to happen later but nothing needed defining at that point in time. I think one of those present actually came up with the Laste Unit. I don't think the original proposal was mine. I think it was one of the soldiers, one of the officers, who had spent some time fighting alongside that unit, and they requested that particular unit as assistance, which I didn't oppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Do you remember which officer that was?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think I could possibly remember. Those were just talks. It wasn't like someone was being interviewed or interrogated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You were aware at all times that that video -- that that meeting was being videoed and that wasn't anything secret. That was quite open that it was being videoed. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I think I didn't. I believe that I didn't think at the time that the meeting was being videotaped at the time -- or perhaps I did. It didn't matter. That's what I think. I think the meeting was being videotaped. There was the military information service there and I think they were taping the meeting, but I'm not sure about the context, to be quite specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's okay.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an awareness, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. All right. But just to continue with the document on your screen there, would you agree with me -- feel free to look at it if you need to, but I'll put to you the proposition, and the Prosecutor can interrupt if it's wrong, that that document, the Zenica Conclusions document of the 29th of August, doesn't make any reference to Sefer Halilovic being appointed to command any operation in Mostar or in the region surrounding Mostar. And what I'd ask you is this: Are you entirely certain that in the discussions at Zenica, General Halilovic really was made the commander of any operation in that area? Given what's on the tape, given what's in the evidence of Mr. Gusic, given what's on -- what's not in the document before you, what's your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that I think that I said before that I didn't understand that anyone was appointed at that meeting by name, that any operation was defined under any specific name or even a plan. It was my understanding that all these things would happen; that's as much as I gathered at the meeting itself. But I understood nothing about what you're suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. After the Zenica meeting, did your duties involve you holding any further conferences or formal discussions with Commander Delic concerning any operations in Herzegovina prior to the departure of the Laste Unit?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that we held any talks on that occasion in order to make matters more specific. The officers stayed in the meeting and I left to attend to my other duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And in subsequent days, was it any part of your duty to speak to Commander Delic about military operations in the Herzegovina area, and the time period I'm asking you about is between Zenica and the departure of the Laste in the early days of September?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't my duty to talk to Delic. Normally we didn't discuss military operations. I remained duty-bound, or rather I had accepted the duty as soon as the time was set for the special unit to be in a certain place that the unit would be dispatched according to the plan. But I assume you're thinking about -- or rather, you're saying -- well, we didn't talk, nor did I talk to anyone else later about any possible plans for any activities or the operation, the way it's defined here. We are treating it as the Neretva operation. No, I didn't talk about that plan or about any other military activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. And on the question of the Laste and its resubordination, who was it who ultimately drafted the -- any order concerning the moving of that unit down to Mostar? Was that Munir Alibabic who did that?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Alibabic that wrote the order for the unit to be sent. I think that order must exist because that was the order followed by the unit command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, I think you confirmed that you, yourself, had not seen this order, but in what archives might that order be expected to be found?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be in the archives of the security services centre in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps -- or if I may be of any further assistance in this context, as they say, you should go and look. It might be in the archives of the special unit, which again is part of the security services centre archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. And although I'm jumping forward to Mostar briefly, it's in relation to the Laste Unit. In Mostar at the CSB at that time -- sorry, perhaps if you could just explain to the Judges what the CSB is.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's an abbreviation for security services centre, which is an organisational unit within the Ministry of the Interior covering a region, an area, in which there are further police stations. There could be anywhere from three to ten or 11 police stations in the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in the case of the Mostar CSB, there was a man named Maslesa, M-a-s-l-e-s-a. What was his position at the CSB?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the chief of the security services centre, the CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: There was another man called Alica Bilic. What was his position?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Alica was an employee of the state security service in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: A man named Sejad Brankovic. Do you recall him and what was his position?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he, too, was an employee of the state security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And was he, too, based in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say whether he was in Mostar. The CSB covers a large area, so he could have been based in Jablanica, Konjic, or anywhere else, although his -- the institution that he belonged to was certainly based in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, my question was imprecise and you have repaired it. Thank you for that answer. Well, now, returning to the issue of the Laste, it's -- in terms of the order, are you now able to say what date it was that the Laste actually set off?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really state anything about the dates with full certainty. The unit must have left Sarajevo on or about the 4th or the 5th of September, but I couldn't be more specific than that. I couldn't tell you where they were at a particular time because I didn't closely monitor its departure. All I'm saying is that my visit to Mostar coincided in time with the travel of the unit to Mostar. We, in fact, travelled together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. It may be possible to build a chronology by reference to some other events. Did you come out through the tunnel yourself on an occasion when you were passing through the tunnel and you met Sefko Hodzic, a journalist, and Sefer Halilovic going back into Sarajevo for a brief visit on or about the 5th of September?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: This being a chance meeting, as you passed through the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, but I can't be certain because we would meet in many places, on many occasions. Our meetings were frequent. We had many activities together, so I couldn't be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that. We have had such evidence from Mr. Hodzic that this was a -- just a passing meeting, accidental and probably of no consequence, but that it took place on the evening or night of the 5th of September. Do you have any comment to make about that beyond saying that it's possible it happened? Do you have any specific recollection that you can help with or not?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's okay. Did the Laste leave before you or after you?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say. I don't know when they left because their departure had to be planned in advance because they're quite a large formation, and it's quite a different matter when an individual travels. It's arranged in different way. So I couldn't tell you anything more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Can you say whether the Laste Unit came to be billeted at Konjic on the way down?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know where they were billeted. All I know is that their first destination was in Tarcin because some other members of the unit were waiting for them there. This is where the two parts of the unit linked up. They had their own plans detailing their travel, their billeting. This was done in the assistance with lower formation, because after all this involved 50 people and they couldn't just sleep anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Of course. And who had the responsibility -- you don't have to provide a name if you can't remember. But what organisation and what officers had the responsibility to arrange transport and accommodation for the Laste Unit as they made their way down towards Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR ALISPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that what you're talking about now is specified in the document dispatching the unit. Normally such a document will specify who exactly will provide accommodation for the unit and so on. Therefore, I couldn't tell you whether it was the police station that they reported to or some military command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
